summary: Defines a profile of Static Context Header Compression and Fragmentation (SCHC, RFC 8724) for LoRaWAN. It shows how to apply SCHC's generic compression and fragmentation to this low-power wide-area technology, whose messages are very small.

eli5.summary: LoRaWAN messages are tiny. This shows how to shrink Internet headers and slice larger messages so they still fit.

questions: how to send ipv6 over lorawan
how does schc use the lorawan fport
what ruleid values does schc over lorawan recommend
subtitle: How to squeeze IPv6 headers and slice large packets so they fit into tiny LoRaWAN frames.

tldr.problem: LoRaWAN frames are very small and devices must save power, so full IPv6 and UDP headers do not fit well. The generic SCHC framework of RFC 8724 leaves many parameters open.
tldr.mechanism: This profile fixes those parameters for LoRaWAN. The RuleID travels in the 8-bit LoRaWAN FPort field, uplink fragments use ACK-on-Error with 10-byte tiles, and downlink fragments use ACK-Always with a window of one tile.
tldr.outcome: Devices and SCHC gateways can interoperate with the same recommended RuleIDs (20, 21 and 22), a privacy-friendly IID algorithm, and clear timer defaults.

today: RFC 9011 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on the generic framework in RFC 8724.

sections.title: Why SCHC Needs a LoRaWAN Profile
sections.content:
SCHC (Static Context Header Compression and Fragmentation, RFC 8724) is a generic toolbox for Low-Power Wide Area Networks (LPWANs). It has two parts: SCHC C/D (compression and decompression) removes header information that both ends already know, and SCHC F/R (fragmentation and reassembly) cuts a packet into pieces that fit a small and possibly variable MTU.

LPWAN technologies share many traits, but they differ in payload sizes and reactiveness. For efficient performance, parameters and modes of operation must be set for each technology. This document does that for LoRaWAN, which is specified by the LoRa Alliance. How the compression context is exchanged or pre-provisioned is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A toolbox is only useful if you pick the right tools for the job. This RFC picks the right settings for one kind of tiny radio network.

sections.title: LoRaWAN Roles and Device Classes
sections.content:
The RFC maps the generic LPWAN roles onto LoRaWAN. Devices are LoRaWAN end devices, the radio gateway is the LoRaWAN Gateway, and the network gateway is the LoRaWAN Network Server. SCHC C/D and F/R run on the end device and on the LoRaWAN Application Server, which is called the SCHC gateway. It acts as the first-hop IP router for the device. The LPWAN-AAA server is the LoRaWAN Join Server.

LoRaWAN defines three device classes. All devices implement Class A: the device transmits whenever it wants, and the network can only reply in the two receive windows (RX1 and RX2) that follow an uplink. Class B adds scheduled listen windows, trading power for lower downlink latency. Class C keeps the receiver open whenever the device is not transmitting, at a higher power cost. Class B and Class C are mutually exclusive.

Devices use a 32-bit DevAddr over the air, which may not be unique. Towards the SCHC gateway, the network identifies a device by its unique 64-bit DevEUI. SCHC does not require LoRaWAN Confirmed frames, because SCHC has its own acknowledgments.
sections.eli5: Some devices only listen right after they speak, like someone who only checks the mailbox after posting a letter. Others listen on a schedule, and some always keep an ear open but use more battery.

sections.title: FPort as the RuleID
sections.content:
LoRaWAN frames carry an 8-bit frame port field, FPort, with usable values from 1 to 223. This profile reuses it: the FPort is part of the SCHC Message, and the SCHC C/D and F/R concatenate the FPort with the LoRaWAN payload to rebuild the message. The RuleID is therefore 8 bits and lives in the FPort, which saves a byte of payload.

To improve interoperability the RFC recommends three values: RuleID 20 for uplink fragmentation (FPortUp), 21 for downlink fragmentation (FPortDown), and 22 for packets where no compression rule matched. FPortUp MUST differ from FPortDown. A RuleID outside the fragmentation set means fragmentation is not used, so the message goes straight to SCHC C/D. An application can send non-SCHC traffic on other FPort values.

A set of FPort values is required for each SCHC gateway a device talks to, and the way contexts are distributed is outside the scope of the document. All padding bits MUST be 0.
sections.eli5: The port number on each message doubles as a label saying which rulebook to use for unpacking it. Using a label that is already there means no extra bytes are wasted.

sections.title: Computing the Interface Identifier
sections.content:
To avoid the risks described in RFC 8064 and RFC 8065, implementations MUST implement, and SHOULD use, a specific way to derive the IPv6 Interface Identifier (IID). The key is the LoRaWAN AppSKey, and the IID is the first 8 bytes of aes128_cmac(AppSKey, DevEUI), using the AES-CMAC algorithm of RFC 4493.

Because the AppSKey is renewed at each join or rejoin, the IID changes over time, which limits location tracking and correlation. The AppSKey adds entropy, which mitigates address scans, and the IID has no correlation with the hardware DevEUI, so an attacker cannot use the manufacturer OUI to target devices.

A small chance of IID collision exists. If it happens, the device can be rekeyed at layer 2 by triggering a LoRaWAN join. Implementations that use another IID source MUST ensure the device and the SCHC gateway share the same IID.
sections.eli5: Each device gets a nickname made by scrambling its serial number with a secret that changes every time it reconnects. Nobody can guess the maker or follow the device around from the nickname.

sections.title: Uplink Fragmentation
sections.content:
When a device sends a packet too large for one frame, SCHC fragmentation uses the ACK-on-Error reliability mode. The L2 word size is 1 byte. The profile sets: no DTag (size 0, so no interleaved datagrams on one FPort), a 2-bit window index (4 windows), a 6-bit FCN (so up to 63 tiles per window), 10-byte tiles, and the recommended RCS algorithm of RFC 8724. The SCHC header is 16 bits including FPort, so payload overhead is 8 bits. The resulting maximum is 4 windows * 63 tiles * 10 bytes = 2520 bytes.

The last tile may travel in a regular fragment, alone in the All-1 fragment, or either, but the sender MUST make sure the receiver does not get it both ways in one session. Timers default to a RECOMMENDED 12 hours for retransmission and for inactivity, and MAX_ACK_REQUESTS is 8.

For battery-powered devices, the RFC recommends an ACK after every window, even if no tile is missing, and that the sender waits for it before the next window, sending a SCHC ACK REQ if needed. This avoids useless uplinks when the device has lost coverage. For devices that are not battery powered, the receiver MAY send an ACK only after all windows, which reduces downlink load. Implementations MUST support both behaviours.
sections.eli5: A big letter is cut into small pieces of the same size. After each batch the receiver says what arrived. Devices on batteries check in more often so they do not waste energy shouting into the void.

sections.title: Downlink Fragmentation and Timers
sections.content:
In the other direction the SCHC gateway fragments and the device reassembles. Unicast downlinks use ACK-Always. Multicast downlinks use No-ACK, with reliability left to the upper layer; this is optional for the gateway and required for the device. The FCN is 1 bit (window size of 1 tile) and the window index is 1 bit. Since only one tile is used, its size follows the currently available MTU. The SCHC header is 10 bits including FPort.

A Class A device can only receive after an uplink, so the gateway cannot start a session on its own. The RFC recommends that Class A devices send an uplink, preferably an empty LoRaWAN frame, every 24 hours when no session is active, to open a downlink opportunity. The gateway inactivity timer for Class A is RECOMMENDED at 36 hours, and the retransmission timer at INACTIVITY_TIMER/(MAX_ACK_REQUESTS + 1).

For Class B the retransmission timer is 3 times the ping slot periodicity, and for Class C it is 30 seconds. The inactivity timer is 12 hours for both. The LoRaWAN FPending bit SHOULD NOT be used for SCHC.
sections.eli5: Going the other way, the pieces come one at a time and the device confirms each one. Because some devices only listen after they speak, they are told to say a quick hello once a day so the network has a chance to answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document only provides parameters for RFC 8724 on LoRaWAN, so it adds no new security issues beyond those already identified there. IID security is covered by the algorithm described above.

SCHC data in the LoRaWAN payload is protected at the LoRaWAN level by AES-128 encryption with a session key shared by the device and the SCHC gateway. Those session keys are renewed at each LoRaWAN session, meaning each join or rejoin. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The messages are already locked by LoRaWAN, and the lock key is swapped for a new one each time the device reconnects. This RFC adds no new weak spots.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The appendix walks through three cases. In the first, 78 bytes of application data compress with Rule 1 to 40 bytes and 5 bits (1 byte RuleID, 21 bits residue, 37 bytes payload). With a 51-byte LoRaWAN MTU and 2-byte FOpts, 49 bytes are available, so no fragmentation is needed.

In the second, 300 bytes compress to 282 bytes and 5 bits and must be fragmented over several uplinks using RuleID 20, ending with an All-1 message carrying a 4-byte RCS and a SCHC ACK from the receiver. In the third, 155 bytes compress to 130 bytes and 5 bits and are sent as downlinks using RuleID 21, each acknowledged by the device.
sections.eli5: The examples show a short note that fits in one go, and longer notes cut into pieces with a thumbs-up after each batch.
